content: Opal is a mineraloid gel that forms at relatively low temperatures and is commonly found in the fissures of various types of rocks, including limonite, sandstone, rhyolite, and basalt. Its water content typically ranges from 3% to 10%, but it can reach up to 20%. Opals exhibit a wide spectrum of colors, including clear, white, gray, red, orange, yellow, green, blue, magenta, rose, pink, slate, olive, brown, and black. Among these, red opals against a black background are the rarest and most valuable, while white and green opals are the most common. The color variations are influenced by the growth size of the silica spheres within the opal, which affect the wavelengths of light reflected, particularly in the red and infrared spectrum. Common opal is amorphous, lacking a defined internal structure, whereas precious opal has a structural element. Precious opal is composed of silica spheres, typically 150 to 300 nanometers in diameter, arranged in a hexagonal or cubic close-packed lattice. This ordered arrangement of silica spheres causes the diffraction and interference of light, producing the characteristic play of color seen in precious opals. The quality of the play of color depends on the uniformity of the sphere sizes and their packing. The phenomenon can be explained by Bragg's Law of diffraction, where the spacing and orientation of the silica planes determine the observed colors. The term play of color is the correct description of this optical effect, while opalescence refers to the milky or turbid appearance of common opal, which lacks the play of color. Opals are often prepared as gemstones using methods like doublets and triplets. A doublet opal consists of a thin layer of opal backed by a dark material such as ironstone, basalt, or obsidian, which enhances the play of color. A triplet opal includes a domed cap of clear quartz or plastic on top of the opal layer, providing protection and magnifying the play of color. However, triplet opals are considered less natural and are not classified as precious opals. Common opals include varieties such as milk opal (milky bluish to greenish), resin opal (honey-yellow with a resinous luster), wood opal (formed by the replacement of organic material in wood with opal), menilite (brown or gray), hyalite (colorless and glass-clear), geyserite (deposited around hot springs or geysers), and diatomite (accumulations of diatom shells). Fire opals are transparent to translucent opals with warm body colors like yellow, orange, or red, but they do not exhibit a play of color. The most famous source of fire opals is the state of Querétaro in Mexico, often referred to as Mexican fire opals. Peruvian opals, also known as blue opals, are semi-opaque to opaque blue-green stones found in Peru, often cut to include the matrix. Australia is the leading producer of opals, accounting for approximately 97% of the world's supply. The majority are light opals (white and crystal opals), with black opals and boulder opals being less common. Major Australian opal-producing regions include Coober Pedy, Andamooka, and Lightning Ridge. Other notable sources of opals include the Virgin Valley in Nevada, Spencer in Idaho, and various locations worldwide, such as the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Turkey, Indonesia, Brazil, Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, and Ethiopia. In 2008, NASA announced the discovery of opal deposits on Mars. Synthetic opals have been produced both experimentally and commercially. The ordered sphere structure of precious opals was first synthesized by Pierre Gilson in 1974. Synthetic opals can be distinguished from natural opals by their regularity, lack of fluorescence under UV light, lower density, and higher porosity. Notable producers of synthetic opals include Kyocera and Inamori of Japan. Vintage imitation opals, such as Slocum Stone, are made of laminated glass with interspersed foil. The atomic structure of opals is unique. As a mineraloid, opals lack a unit cell, and their structure can range from amorphous to microcrystalline. Amorphous opals, such as opal-A, consist of aggregated silica spheres with water filling the spaces between them. Microcrystalline opals, such as opal-CT, contain clusters of cristobalite and tridymite blades. Over time, non-crystalline opals can transform into more ordered forms like opal-CT and opal-C due to diagenesis under increasing pressure in sedimentary rocks. Historically, opals were considered symbols of great luck in the Middle Ages, believed to possess the virtues of all gemstones due to their multicolored appearance. However, modern superstitions associate opals with bad luck, unless they are the owner's birthstone (October) or given as a gift. The fragility of opals compared to other gemstones may have contributed to their negative reputation. In popular culture, opals are the official gemstone of South Australia, the Commonwealth of Australia, and Nevada. They are also the traditional birthstone for October.
